title: The sham-lawyer, or, The lucky extravagant as it was damnably acted at the Theatre-Royal in Drury-Lane.
author: Drake, James, 1667-1707.

speeches.speaker: Friend.
prose:
PRithee dear Careless consider a little, and try to manage the last
Stake, I'm no great Friend to plodding business, but thy Extravagance
makes me Grave: I'm asham'd to see thee thus varying
thy outside continually like a Camelion, a few days will
reduce thee to the same Diet too.

speeches.speaker: Carel.
prose:
Yes, yes, i'm like to edifie by such a Preacher, whose life's a continu'd
contradiction to his Doctrine, now art thou 'tis ten to one going to a
Whore and a Treat, and recommend'st thrift to me, only to give the better
relish to thy own iniquity, like a Pamper'd Chaplain's preaching Abstinence,
and surfeiting all the time on the Luxury of his Lords's Table.

speeches.speaker: Friend.
prose:
A wise Gamster need not absolutely forswear Play; but I'm mad to
see you a. Bubble to your own Indiscretion; and in a world so full of Sharpers
thinking you play upon the Square.

speeches.speaker: Carel.
prose:
Hang Caution, 'tis the Companion of Fools; I tell thee Friendly, that
among all the numerous Follies of Mankind, there's none so ridiculous, and
so destructive to our ease as that which they call Discretion, 'tis a Bridle put
into the mouths of Asses, by which they are ridden, and manag'd to other
Mens Humours; I defie it, and from hence forward Wit be my Wealth, and
Pleasure my Business.

speeches.speaker: Friend.
prose:
Pleasure and Wit are Mistresses that must be treated high, a Poor
Lover can no more hope a Favour from either, than from a Town-Jilt, or a
Courtier; 'tis never Flood with them, when the Pocket is at low E^. If
you wou'd preserve their Favour, keep your Estate, when that's gone you'l
find they'l soon desert you.

speeches.speaker: Carel.
prose:
Does true Wealth then consist only in the number of Acres? No let
the dull Landed Clods manure the Dirt they sprang from, and when they^ve
worn themselves out in the Slavery, fatten it with a Dung-hill of their
own Carcases; I cultivate a more fruitful Soil; my Brains my Estate;
my Wit my Plow; Pleasure my Crop; the whole Town my Tenants; the
Tavern my Store-house; every Man's Purse my Exchequer; thine or any
Friends Wardrobe mine; and your Houses (when I please) my Lodging. Thus
I've given a Particular of my Revenue, acquir'd without Purchase; enjoy'd
without Settlement; and collected without trouble; My Friends are all my
Stewards; for what one brave Spirit enjoys is common to all; Nature and
great Souls know no limits; they scorn the mean distinctions of Meum & Tuum.

speeches.speaker: Friend.
prose:
You've spent your Estate to a fine Purpose, and are in a fair way to
make a Philosopher, a Diogenes the second; pray reserve a Tub for a habitation,
th^ you may secure some retreat at last. It vexes me to see you so easie and
ca^eless, as to hug those that devour you: No raw Squire was ever fonder of
the Rooks that made a Cully of him; or thought 'em civiller Gentlemen for
supplying him with Money to cheat him of it again.

speeches.speaker: Carel.
prose:
Faith! He that has any such designs against me may cheat himself;
me he can't. When I had my Estate I was plagu'd with a Nursery of Beggars,
call'd Footmen; kept Hospitals for Curs and Kites; and Muster'd Regiments
of Fools and Knaves every day at my Table; that surfeited on my Folly,
and paid with a Country Proverb, God bless the F^under.

speeches.speaker: Friend.
prose:
That was your Fault, and is so still; must you needs sacrifice to
Knaves, or Fools? Cou'd you not avoid the Caterpillars of the Country, that
only devour'd the Fruit, but you must harbour worse Vermine here, that
will consume the Land, and prey at last, like Lice upon your Body?

speeches.speaker: Carel.
prose:
'Tis Nature's fault (if it be one) that made me a Lover of Mirth and
Pleasure, not Business. I find my self a Sociable Creature with natural Appetites
about me; those I gratifie; a Prince can do no more; then why shou'd I
by an unnecessary solicitude disturb the quiet enjoyment of 'em.

speeches.speaker: Friend.
Carel.
prose:
What different notions Men have of things! What you call Extravagance
was the height of Policy in me. I examin'd all my Nature's demands,
and found I had no occasion for 3000l. a year, why then should I be encumber'd
with it? A Snail's happier in's Shell, than if he had all Versailles upon
his Back. I resolv'd therefore to turn the Tables, and make other Men my
Proveditors, as I had been theirs.

speeches.speaker: Friend.
Carel.
prose:
Hang 'em Locusts (do you think I mean my Creditors?) If the
World were an absolute Wilderness, I wou'd starve e're I wou'd prey upon
such Insects. No, I mean those Gentlemen, my Friends, that have been as
free with me, and are sensible of their Obligations.

speeches.speaker: Friend.
prose:
Friends, that are sensible of Obligations! where do those Monsters
grow? Has all thy Wit, and thy dear bought Experience taught thee to know

the World no better? Don't you know that Friends are a sort of Summer-Companions,
that leave you at the first approach of Winter, and that to oblige
a Man, is a sure way to make him shun you, when your necessities begin
to call for a return?

speeches.speaker: 1st. Ten.
prose: There he is, let's lay it home to him.

speeches.speaker: 2d. Ten.
prose:
I'le warrant you, a Paper-mill shall be silence to me.
Sir, an't like your Worship, here be some of your poor Tenants—

speeches.speaker: Carel.
prose:
'Tis a Lye, and does n't like my Worship, you're no Tenants of
mine. Wou'd Yee have an abatement of your Rent for Repairs, or Taxes?
March into the City, there are those that love to be troubled with you.

speeches.speaker: 1st. Ten.
prose: We beseech you, Sir, don't be undone for your own Good.

speeches.speaker: Carel.
prose:
Sirrah, whistle to your Horses, and let them edifie, and trouble
your empty Noddle no more with my Good.

speeches.speaker: 2d. Ten.
prose:
We beseech you, Sir, consider our hard case, We shall be turn'd
out of Doors; pity us, as we do you: Say what we must do.

speeches.speaker: Carel.
prose:
Sow Hemp, and hang your selves with it, Rascals; or go, and fawn
upon your new Landlord, flatter his sordid Covetousness, call it thrift, and
rail at my Prodigality, and witness his Forgeries. You look like thriving
Knaves, he'l find you Employment as Knights of the Post; and that may
prefer you to the Pillory; those superfluous Lugs of yours well prun'd may
yeild you as great a Crop, and bring you as much Dirt (since you're so fond
of it) as my Farms. Or, if you'd rather, take a Purse, and let the Gallows
provide for you the shortest way; your Countenances will become a Halter,
and a Psalm. There's advice for you: No Replies, but vanish. Am I so low
as your pity, Slaves?

speeches.speaker: 1st. Ten.
prose:
Good Sir, have Compassion on Us for our Wives, and poor Children's
sakes.

speeches.speaker: Carel.
prose:
Who bid you get 'em? Ha'n't you Threshing Work enough, but
Children must be bang'd out of the Sheaf too? Our Beau's, with all their
Strengtheners get nothing but Diseases; But these Rogues, Friendly, upon a
Clove of Garlick, a piece of hard Cheese that wou'd starve the Rats, and
break a Saw, and a little sowre Milk, can mount like Stallions; and expect I
shou'd maintain these Tumblers.

speeches.speaker: Friend.
prose:
Whatever thou hast for the Children, thou dost n't use to want
Compassion for the Women; pray take 'em into Consideration.

speeches.speaker: Carel.
prose:
D'yee hear Fellows, your Wives I think may be wholesome, send
'em to me, and I'l teach 'em Trades they shall live by; as for the Brats, let
the Parish, that club'd to beget 'em, join to maintain 'em.

speeches.speaker: 1st Ten.
prose: Sir, your Father's Worship wou'd ha'us'd us better?

speeches.speaker: Carel.
prose:
My Father's Worship was an Ass for using you at all, else he had
ne'r left me the Plague of such an Estate, which I have parted with to get
rid of you.

speeches.speaker: 2d. Ten.
prose:
Nay, an' you abuse us thus, you must bear with us, if we tell
You your own. Pray, what maintain'd your Whores, and supplied your riotous
Extravagance? Who found you Money for the Gaming-Ordinaries,
and paid your Tavern, Taylor's and Surgeon's Bills? Our Labour sure. For
without it, all you Father's Estate wou'd have afforded you no better Fare,
than your Horse has.

speeches.speaker: 1st. Ten.
prose:
Your Father, rest his Soul, kept a noble House, and bid his Friends
and Neighbours welcome to good Meat and Drink; kept good Horses,
Hounds and Hawks; and cou'd hunt a whole Summer's morning in his own
Grounds; and all this he thought himself beholding to our honest Industry
for, that brought him in good Rents.

speeches.speaker: Carel.
prose:
Dogs, do you remonstrate, you sawcy Puppies? You that were necessary
to his Estate indeed, but like the Dung, that lay upon it, a necessary
Nusance that made it rich and nasty; that were company only for his
Dogs, and liv'd like 'em upon the Reversions of his Table.

speeches.speaker: 2d. Ten.
prose:
Those Dogs liv'd better, and at more liberty, than you'l do in a
little Time; in the Kings-Bench you'l think that Dung-Civet, and wish for
those dirty Acres to take the Air in, and these Dogs to wait upon you.

speeches.speaker: Carel.
prose: Rascals, Villains, I'l teach you Manners.

speeches.speaker: Friend.
prose:
Begone, honest Friends, you've heated him, and the next time let
your Zeal be more respectful.

speeches.speaker: 1st. Ten.
prose:
Yes, we'l go, but it shall be like Rams to return with greater
force; We'l teize him into Reason.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose: Is your Mortgage past Redemption, Careless?

speeches.speaker: Carel.
prose:
Faith, I think not, but 'tis as bad, for I've neither Money nor Inclination
to redeem it.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose:
I've both, and you shall n't part with't so: Shall that Rogue insult us
both, get my Mistress from me first, and then your Estate?

speeches.speaker: Carel.
prose:
We may be bound to thank him for both, as we may manage matters,
and make him keep a Mistress for you, and gather Rents for me.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose:
That's my present aim, which I miss, if, tho' the Lawyer hold the
Plow, the Crop ben't of my Sowing; thither I'm bound this minute.

speeches.speaker: Carel.
prose:
'Tis a laudable Design; but why in this trim, Thou that usest to
out-brave the Spring? A green Bag wou'd become thee better now, than a
Billet-Doux; Love's Merchants shou'd all be gay Adventurers.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose:
There's a Mystery in that, a little time will unriddle to you. But here
comes the Pilot, that must conduct me into the wish'd Harbour.

speeches.speaker: Carel.
prose:
Faith, I like thy Fancy, of making the Spirit Pimp for the Flesh,
very well; these Spiritual Guides seldom miss the way to the Carnal Part;
these Conscience-Brokers, these Scruple-Mongers are the best Bellows to blow
such Flames with; and this of 'em all the fittest Engine in Europe for your
purpose: For he has as little Conscience as Learning, but 'tis as craving as
his Stomach, and govern'd by't; a Treat, or a Bribe makes him your Creature.

speeches.speaker: Hom.
prose:
Hard Times, Spade, very hard Times; we pray, and pray, but to little
purpose; formerly, if a good warm Sermon wou'd n't kindle Men's Zeal,
it wou'd their Fires, and Men of our Function were sure of two or three
good Meals at least in a Week gratis; now, in spight of all we can say, their
Kitchins are as cool as their Charities.

speeches.speaker: Spade.
prose:
Nay, if you complain, Sir, what may we poor Sextons do, that live
upon the bare Sound of Prayers? We rise, and ring the Bells, and get good
Stomachs, and may eat the Ropes when we've done to satisfie 'em.

speeches.speaker: Hom.
prose:
We us'd to earn now and then a comfortable Ten Shilings by

Preaching an old Sermon, but our Benefic'd-Men are grown so provident,
that they buy 'em ready Printed as cheap as we can, and preach 'em themselves.
When had we a Christning, Spade?

speeches.speaker: Spade.
prose:
Not this ten Weeks: they've gi'n o're getting Children: The Taxes,
the Seas, and Usury undo us, take off their Edges, and blunt their Plough-shares.
There are some poor Labourers, that perhaps once in seven years, by
helping one another produce some few puny Butter-Prints, that seldom hold
the Christning without shrinking in the wetting.

speeches.speaker: Hom.
prose:
The young Mad-Caps carry their Diseases into Flanders, there the
Pox, or the Enemy dispatches 'em, and there's the profit of their Burials lost.

speeches.speaker: Spade.
prose:
Ay, and they're grown so hard-hearted of late, that they won't die
at home; and so cheat the King, and the Parson of their Duties. I've buried
but one Man these three Months, and that was an Apothecary that pin'd for
want of Business.

speeches.speaker: Hom.
prose:
'Tis a healthy year, a lamentable healthy year, the Air's too wholsome.
What a torment 'tis to have a slender Stipend, and an Immortal Parish.

speeches.speaker: Spade.
prose:
You're allow'd to pray against all Weathers foul, or fair, as you see
fit, Master; why not against all Airs too, good or bad?

speeches.speaker: Hom.
prose: 'Tis n't i'th' Cannon, Man, I'd give my best Cassock, that it were.

speeches.speaker: Spade.
prose:
'Tis strange! they're starv'd too, yet they won't die here, they
won't Earth. A good Plague now, or half dozen new fantastical Fevers, that
wou'd turn up their Heels by whole sale, and take the Doctors in their grave
Consultations, that there might be no natural help for Money. How merrily
my Bells won'd go then!

speeches.speaker: Hom.
prose:
Hold there, Boy, Doctors and Apothecaries, are our Friends, let's
spare them; For tho they're slow, they're certain. O! for Mr. Bolus, and
Mr. Glister, the two great Apothecaries in our Neighbourhood again, they
did but give 'em a shake, and they dropt like ripe Fruit from the stalk. Now
we must either remove to some muddy air, or wait for a Contagious Season.

speeches.speaker: Spade.
prose:
Oh! for the Hundreds of Essex here, Master, that Nursery of
Agues, Agues that will shake Men's Souls out, and ne'r stay for Drugs, Possets,
or Plaisters.

speeches.speaker: Hom.
prose: Gouts, Rheumatisms, and dead Palsies.—

speeches.speaker: Spade.
prose:
I like that word Dead monstrously: But for those Gouts and Rheumatisms,
they'l hang an Arse a scurvy while. The Pox, Small Pox, or Epidemical
Surfeits are rich Marle, and make a Church-yard fat, and the Sexton merry.

speeches.speaker: Car.
prose:
N'er doubt you Levite, he's as true a Tumbler, as e're
was play'd at a Coney; I'll warrant he fetches her.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose: Prithee leave me now, and anon you shall hear further from me.

speeches.speaker: Car.
prose:
Farewell, and if you want my assistance, send me your Instructions,
and I'll pursue 'em with more Application than ever the Lawyer did a rich
Client's Breviate; I'm a very able Councellor in a case of Cuckoldom.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose: Sir, your most humble Servant, is not your name Homily?

speeches.speaker: Hom.
prose: It is, Sir, your Will with me, I pray?

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose: Are not you Curate of the Neighbouring Parish?

speeches.speaker: Hom.
prose:
I am so, Some Funeral Sermon, or some secret slip to be Baptiz'd,
or some stoln Fortune to be privately married, and conceal'd, Fortune an'^
be thy will.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose: Sir, I've a little business with you at your good leisure.

speeches.speaker: Hom.
prose:
I pray, Sir, be free, if it be matter of Privacy, this Man's my Sexton,
and ^, be trusted.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose:
Sir, O my business is partly with him too, and I am glad to meet you
both so opportun^ly.

speeches.speaker: Hom.
prose:
Well, Sir, I partly guess your Business,—you wou'd be Married, I
suppose,—and desire secrecy, this may be done,—and with security too,—
'tis but antedating the Certificate.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose: There will be no occasion—

speeches.speaker: Hom.
prose:
Excuse me, Sir, I say there will be occasion, give me leave to understand
these matters,—'tis part of my Trade. For without an antedated Certificate,
how will you evade the Act of Parliament, which obliges to a discovery?

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose: You say true, Sir, but my Business is of another nature.

speeches.speaker: Hom.
prose:
Cry you mercy, Sir; Perhaps you've transgrest, and the fruit of it
calls for our Assistance; nay, ne're blush for the matter, young Blood is warm,
and the offence is veni^l, the Lambs of God will play, 'tis best to sow our
wild Oats in our Youth, we make the better Christians for't after. Here's my
Sexton too, if you've occasion, shall for a small Sum oblige the Parish to take
care of it.

speeches.speaker: Spad.
prose:
Or if you wou'd quit your Hands of the Mother, for Forty Shillings,
I'll bring one that shall Marry her, and so rid you at once of both, if
she be yet undeliver'd.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose: I thank you both, Gentlemen, but you're wide of the matter still.

speeches.speaker: Hom.
prose:
Have you lost any Relation, or Friend, and wou'd have a Funeral
Sermon? I shall be very reasonable: For a Father 40s. shall suffice, a Mother,
Brother, or Sister 30s. an Uncle, or Aunt 20s. and for a Friend, or more
distant Relation 10s. Say your Price, and it shall be done accordingly.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose:
Still you prevent me, Sir; but to be short, my Business is from an Old
Friend of your's in New England.

speeches.speaker: Hom.
prose:
A Friend in New England! Sir, I know no Body there: His Name
pray, and Business?

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose: That Letter there will inform you of both.

speeches.speaker: Spad.
prose:
Have a care of a Trick, Master; He looks like a Sharper, I don't
like him.

speeches.speaker: Hom.
prose:
Ne'r fear, Cantabit Vacuus, all I've to lose is my Learning, and that
he may put in a Nut-shell.

SIR,

SINCE my Settling in New England I've sent several Letters to you to desire
a Correspondence, and a continuance of our Ancient Friendship; But never
receiving any Answer, I have doubted either your Death or Removal from London,
or at least the miscarriage of all my Letters. For I cou'd not persuade my self that
either length of Time, or distance of Place cou'd discard from the Memory or Affections
a Friend so early, and so deeply rooted in 'em: I conjure you therefore by that
strict and mutual intimacy contracted in our Youth, and so long continued (till that
necessary to my Affairs, but cruel divorce forc'd me from you hither about twenty
years since) to take care of this Young Man my Son, the Bearer, and see him plac'd

under the Care and instruction of some able, experienc'd, and sober Lawyer; and in
so doing you shall not only make amends for your past forgetfulness, but further oblige
an acknowledging as well as

Your real and hearty Friend,
TRADEWELL.

speeches.speaker: Hom.
prose:
New England—Several Letters—Ancient Friendship—Tradewell—
A very ancient Friend sure! For the Duce a Man of that Name can I remember
in New or Old England!

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose: You look, as if you had forgot my Father, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Hom.
prose: No, I look as if I wou'd remember; for I can't forget what I never knew.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose:
I've heard my Father say, You were Students, and Chamber-fellows together
in Oxford, till he Married.

speeches.speaker: Hom.
prose:
'Tis impossible, Young Man, I'm a perfect Stranger to the Name,
and have no more acquaintance in New England than in Catay.

speeches.speaker: Spad.
prose:
Look sharp, Master, this Fellow wou'd banter us out of our Wits.
D'ye hear Friend, have you no Letters for me?

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose:
No Letters, but I was charg'd by my Father to give his Love to honest
Old Spade the merry Sexton, if you be he.

speeches.speaker: Spad.
prose:
Hah! have I unknown Friends too? Hark ye, Young Man, what
time o'th' Moon is't? Ha'ye been worm'd since ye came over? If I know
your Father, or any of your Kin, hang me in my own Bell-Ropes.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose:
Gentlemen, I thank you, I was told you were the Men; but it may be
my Father's Friends are dead, and you of the same Names succeed 'em. You
do honestly to undeceive me; For I had a Present of 60 Pistols to deliver to
them, as a Token of my Father's Love, but since you are n't the Men.

speeches.speaker: Hom.
prose:
Pray, Sir, have a little Patience, and let me think, pray stay a little,
and let me remember, it vexes me to forget an Old Friend, an intimate Friend.

speeches.speaker: Spad.
prose: A kind Friend too, that sends so lovingly, Master.

speeches.speaker: Hom.
prose:
We hard Students have very slippery Memories; but we must be the
Persons: For he and I have been Curate and Sexton in this Parish these 35
Years. I must remember sure.

speeches.speaker: Spad.
prose: Pray remember, Master, such Friends are not to be forgotten.

speeches.speaker: Hom.
prose:
Stay, methinks I have him now, let me see a goodly, proper, strait,
well timber'd, grave Gentleman with—

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose: Black Hair.

speeches.speaker: Hom.
prose:
Very right, with a goodly Beard, when he was in England he liv'd
next Door to the—

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose: To the Sign of the Holy Lamb hard by this Place.

speeches.speaker: Spad.
prose:
Alack, alack, what Squire Tradewell, Master? Oh 'twas a Noble
Gentlem^n.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose: ^-a-mercy Letter, now it operates.

speeches.speaker: Hom.
prose:
^ee what a Treacherous Knave this Time is; how has he play'd the
Wag ^ me, to make me forget my best, my dearest Friend? He Married,
let ^—

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose:
^

^e^lthy's Daughter.

speeches.speaker: Hom.
prose:
^ very same, I Married 'em, I remember your Mother perfectly
well, as if it were but Yesterday, a Goodly Lady she was. Oh! the Feasting,
the Masks, the Mirth, we had at that Wedding.

speeches.speaker: Friend.
prose:
How this Money rubs up their Memories! For Ten Pistols more
they'd make her the Great Mogul's Daughter.

speeches.speaker: Hom.
prose:
Your Father and I had both one Soul. Look Spade, whose Eyes are
those? Look in's Face, if he ben't the very Picture of Squire Tradewell. I
think you was born here.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose: I was about five Years old, when he carried me over with him.

speeches.speaker: Hom.
prose: Your Name is—

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose: Samuel.

speeches.speaker: Hom.
prose:
That was your ^ather's Name, I think, Well Gentleman I Baptiz'd
you, and a sweet Child you were then; See now, Time, that consumes us,
shoots him up still sweeter.

speeches.speaker: Spad.
prose:
A wondrous sweet Child you were, I've kiss'd ye, and play'd with
ye, and dandled ye in my Arms a hundred, and a hundred times, and swung
ye in my Bell-Ropes; ye lov'd swinging.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose:
Lying Rascals, now their Memories are whetted, if it were for their
purpose, they'd remember Adam's Grand-father.

speeches.speaker: Hom.
prose:
Well, Young Gentleman, You're welcome to your Native Air. How
does the Noble Gentleman, your Father? when will he bless his Country in
his Return?

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose:
Very shortly, Sir; till which Time he entreats your care of me, and
desires you to accept of these fifty Pistols, as a small earnest of his future
Gratitude, and acknowledgments of your Services.

speeches.speaker: Hom.
prose:
Sir, I am bound ever to be his very humble Beadsman, and most assiduous
Orator.

speeches.speaker: Spad.
prose:
Lord, Lord, how Sickness decays our Intellects! This is the very Gentleman,
that before your last long Sickness, when I lay so ill at the same time too,
Master, about two years ago, we us'd constantly to remember in our private
Devotions; that a Fever shou'd have such influence over our Memories!

speeches.speaker: Hom.
prose:
Well, it shall be so no more; I shall ever hence forward remember
him, Good Gentleman.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose:
My Father was us'd to say, that his Neighbour Spade the Sexton was a
very honest, but a wondrous Merry Man, and a Good-fellow; and therefore
desir'd me to give his Love and these Ten Pistols to him.

speeches.speaker: Spad.
prose:
Ah! 'tis my noble, generous Master still; and you shall see I can be
merry as ever upon so joyful news as of his Health.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose:
Thanks to the Gold, for half the Sum more thou'dst sing a Psalm as
merrily at his Execution.

speeches.speaker: Spad.
prose:
Shall's to the Dog and Duck, Master, or to the Whelp and Bacon? there's
a Cup of rare Stingo abroach, such as you love, and as good true Nantz, as e're
was tipt o're Tongue.

speeches.speaker: Hom.
prose:
No, Spade, My Charge has been nicely bred, those Houses are too
mean for his high Keeping: We must have something befitting his fine Stomach.
Step and provide us something at the Rummer. You see, Sir, we aren't
dainty, homely Places and mean Cheer serve us usually; we don't pamper
our selves, we mortifie the Carnal Man, but upon such an extraordinary Occasion
to remember an old loving Friend, and in respect to you Sir.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose:
I humbly thank you, Sir, but it needs not, I'm not delicate, and have at
present no Appetite but to my Study, which must be the Law. I desire you
to excuse me.

speeches.speaker: Spad.
prose:
But, Sir, you may be hungry, you must be hungry, pray do nothing
rashly; Study creates Appetite mainly, but ben't too violent, it impairs the
Health; Take your refreshment first, 'tis time, and then to your Study. Here's
my Master, had n'er been what he is at these years, if he had studied immoderately.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose:
I thank you both for your Care, but I desire you to dispense with me
at this time. But, Sir, I suppose my Father in his Letter has made it his request,
as I do mine, to place me under the Instructions of some Lawyer of
great Business; and for his Pains and Care he shall be gratified with two hundred
Guineas, besides his own demand for my Lodging and Diet. I've heard
much of Serjeant Wrangle.

speeches.speaker: Spade.
prose:
What, not eat, nor drink, first; Sure he has n't heard any thing of
the Serjeant's House keeping yet. Well, he's an Ass, and so we'l use him.
Young Gentleman you shall be a Lawyer, and surfeit upon Cook and Littleton.

speeches.speaker: Hom.
prose:
Sir, You've hit happily upon Serjeant Wrangle, he's an able Councellor,
and makes more noise in Westminster-Hall, than half the Lawyer's there;
he's Master of that Art. He's my near Neighbour and Parishioner, I'll recommend
you to him. See yonder he comes, and Mr. Affidavit, the famous Solicitor,
with him, and one or two more.

speeches.speaker: Wran.
prose:
Well, Gentlemen, you've play'd your Parts to a Miracle, I suppose
we've gi'n 'em their Bellies full of this Cause; they'l know who they
plead (Non est factum) to next time.

speeches.speaker: Aff.
prose:
When I lose a Cause for want of Witnesses, I'll bid adieu to Practice.
as if I cou'd n't prove any Man's Hand when I've a mind to't. Mr. Swearhome
I n'er knew you so out in my life, so shamefully out-sworn, so baff^'d,
by a young Fellow too, that has n't been above five or six years at the Business.

speeches.speaker: Sw.
prose:
Whose Fault was that? I went according to my Instructions: You
knew the merits of the Cause, and shou'd have inform'd me better.

speeches.speaker: Wran.
prose:
He had the disadvantage indeed of being first sworn, but Mr.
Nickit retriev'd all.

speeches.speaker: Sw.
prose:
Ay, he saw where the Pinch was, he swore last, I've known you Mr.
Affidavit, call for the Book ev'n towards the Conclusion of a Cause to no
purpose; if I might ha' had the Book agen, the Cause shou'd n't ha' stuck,
I warrant ye.

speeches.speaker: Wran.
prose:
Come, come Gentlemen, you've all done to admiration, and the
Cause has succeeded accordingly, 't has paid you nobly. Well, a rich Client's
a Blessing: A rich litigious Lord's Cause is an Estate; that's never starv'd:
there are those that expect a Man shou'd drudge for a single Fee, but they
thrive in proportion.

speeches.speaker: Affid.
prose:
Hang the Penurious, their Causes like their Purses have poor Issues.
Good Fees beget good Causes; the Times are Aguish, and a Plea must be
warmly lin'd to keep it in heart.

speeches.speaker: Nick.
prose:
The Prerogative of Crowns goes far, and those that will spare no
cost, need want no Witnesses; experienc'd, fearless Witnesses, that understand
their Businesses, and will make no unnecessary Scruples.

speeches.speaker: Wran.
prose:
Well, Gentlemen, you are all Men of Sagacity in our Business,
and never let a Clause run a-ground upon Truth, but you help it off again

immediately, and set it afloat. I've known Witnesses sometimes over-set a
Cause foully for want of your Discretion: Too much truth is a very bad
Ingredient in a Witness, a little now and then sets a Cause off handsomely,
but laid on too thick, it obscures the Colours, and instead of giving a gloss,
like an ill Varnish it hides all the Beauty. Mr. Swearhome, and Mr, Nicki^,
did my Lord make good his promise to you?

speeches.speaker: Both.
prose:
Very nobly indeed Mr. Serjeant, we're very much oblig'd to you,
and whenever you've occasion, we hope you'l command us in your own
Affairs gratis.

speeches.speaker: Wrang.
prose:
I'm glad on't, my Lord's a wise Man, and knows how to value
your Services. Call upon me anon at my House, I've occasion for your
hands to some Writings, and yours Mr. Affidavit.

speeches.speaker: All.
Hom. and Spade.
prose: A good Morrow to your Worship, Mr. Serjeant.

speeches.speaker: Wrang.
prose:
Thank you Master Homily, thank you good Neighbour Spade. Have
ye any Business with me? if so, be brief, I'm full of Business, and every minute's
precious.

speeches.speaker: Hom.
prose:
We know your Hours are taken up with full Employ, and therefore
have brought this young Gentleman of a considerable Family, and Heir to a
great Estate, and of a promising Aspect.

speeches.speaker: Wrang.
prose: He appears no less; but to what end Neighbours?

speeches.speaker: Hom.
prose: To be your Pupil, Sir, and study the Law under your Instructions.

speeches.speaker: Wrang.
prose:
Alas, Sir, I shou'd be glad to serve you, but I'm a private Man, and
my House strait not fit to receive a man of your Quality, scarce large enough
for my small family, Besides, Sir, you must pardon me, if I be a little scrupulous,
these Times make us all so; I mean you no affront, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
Wrang.
prose:
That's an Honest Pledge, yet there needs none, your Face and Carriage,
Sir, declare an innate honesty.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose:
So strong an Inclination I have to the Law, and hear so great a Character
of you, Sir, that the meanest corner in your House will be more acceptable
to me than a Palace; Books, and your Direction, are all I covet; I shall have
no resort to me, no company; these two are all my acquaintance in this Town.

speeches.speaker: Wrang.
prose:
So much the better; a Student should be retir'd and frugal; to
take you wou'd straighten me very much, my Affairs and the straightness of
my House consider'd. Cou'd you be contented with a hard Lodging in the
Out-parts of my House?

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose: Any thing, Sir, that's dry and wholsome, I'm not wantonly bred.

speeches.speaker: Spad.
prose: Wou'd he'd live with me, and learn to dig?

speeches.speaker: Hom.
prose: Mark but his mind to Learning.

speeches.speaker: Wrang.
prose:
I do, and like it wondrously. Thanks to his Money. He'l
prove a great Lawy^.

speeches.speaker: Hom.
prose: But he's so mod^, Sir, he's too bashful for a Lawyer.

speeches.speaker: Wrang.
prose:
Not at all, 'tis a good Sign. Come, Sir, with me, but you must
keep to your Apartment. Good morrow Neighbours, I thank ye.

speeches.speaker: Hom.
prose:
Good morrow to your Worship, young Gentleman I'll come sometimes,
and crack a Case with you.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose: My good Friends, I thank you both.

speeches.speaker: Hom.
prose:
Fare 'em well, let's to the Tavern Spade, and enjoy our selves, and
pray for the Fool, the Founder.

speeches.speaker: Spad.
prose:
And pray for more such fools, more Friends, and fools from New
England.

speeches.speaker: Hom.
prose:
From Lapland, or whatsoe're quarter the Wind blows Money, I'll
know 'em, instantly, nay, I'll be a-kin to 'em, I can't miss a man that brings Money.

speeches.speaker: Spad.
prose:
I'll change my Trade, Master, and live by the living, let the dead stink,
'tis a poor stinking Trade.

speeches.speaker: Hom.
prose:
If the young fool shou'd chop upon his Wife now, and handle her
Case, that's a Law Point that wou'd make the Lawyer start; 'tis a hidden.
Point worth the canvasing.

speeches.speaker: Spad.
prose:
The Woman was n't born to so much happiness; he's too demure; he
has no heat; Study consumes his Oyl.

speeches.speaker: Hom.
verse: If Fools are doom'd the Favourites of Fate,
Then they that deal with 'em are fortunate.
prose:
I say, if he shou'd sting her home, I shou'd love him for't; for to say
truth, tho' I call him Worshipful, the Lawyer's an arrant Dogbolt, a stingy
narrow sou^d Wretch, that starves the very Rats and Mice out of his House,
and so jealous, that he starts if but the shadow of a man enter at his Window.
I wish him a Cuckold upon Record, and if my Youngster shou'd dub him.—
But let's leave that to the will of Fate, and o're a Cup of lusty Canary let's
Prophesie.

speeches.speaker: Wran.
prose:
LET riotous Prodigals lavish away both health and treasure to please
their wanton Palates, and gorge intemperate Luxury. Let 'em debauch
their Appetites, and consume their Fortunes to purchase Surfeits, and
nurse up diseases; Let 'em be serv'd in Gold and Silver, and indulge themselves
in rich Soups, and costly Ol^o's, in high Ragou's, and nice Fricafsee's till they
grow more lusty and salicious than pamper'd Cardinals; where does this end?
Their Dishes come to us that are wise and provident to pay for their Sawces,
and their Luxurious Carcases either fatten a Church-yard early, or at length
encumber an Hospital. These are the fruits of their excess and vanity, which
the frugal and industrious reap the benefit and comfort of. The wise take
other measures, and know that Nature's content with a little; this Egg to
me's a greater Feast, and contains more Dainties, than French Cook ever
dress'd, or Glutton thought of. In this are health and content, all that wise
Nature asks.

speeches.speaker: Fam.
prose:
I fancy my Nature's none of the wisest then, Sir; for she wou'd never
be satisfied so; yet she knows what's good for her self, and has taught my
Stomach to be more craving.

speeches.speaker: Wrang.
prose:
O' my Conscience thou'st a Wolf in thy Belly, thou insatiable Rascal,
nothing will suffice thy ravenous Gut, I saw you eat two Apples just now:
Prodigious!

speeches.speaker: Fam.
prose:
'T had been a Prodigy indeed, if I had ow'd 'em to your
Liberality.

speeches.speaker: Wrang.
prose:
To feed thee as long as thou'd'st cram, wou'd bring a Dearth upon
the Land; had'st thou been one of the five thousand that were fed by Miracle,
there had been no Fragments brought away; thy Mind's always on thy
Guts, sure thy soul lies there.

speeches.speaker: Fam.
prose:
I can't tell that; but I'm sure 't had need, otherwise they'd shrink up
quite they're so empty; for I get nothing else to put into 'em here.

speeches.speaker: Wrang.
prose:
Ungrateful Rascal, hadn't you the Water I boil'd 'tother Egg in,
to make you hearty Broth? are ye never to be satisfied?

speeches.speaker: Fam.
prose:
Yes, Sir; but I might as soon make the Philosopher's Stone on't.
you gave it me in water, and if 'twere n't for good manners, I cou'd give't
you again in Wind; 'twas so hearty.

speeches.speaker: Wrang.
prose: Hold your tongue, Sirrah! and look to my Egg; how does it roast.

speeches.speaker: Fam,
prose: It heats apace, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Wran.
prose: Turn it then. Where's your Mistress? Why is n't she here?

speeches.speaker: Fam.
prose:
The very sight of this Egg has made him Cockish; what wou'd a
Dozen Butter'd do? She's within, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Wran.
prose: Within, Sir, at what? Is she getting—

speeches.speaker: Fam.
prose: At the Window, getting a good Stomack.

speeches.speaker: Wrang.
prose: I mean, what is she doing, Sirrah?

speeches.speaker: Fam.
prose:
Praying heartily, Sir, upon her knees, that Heaven wou'd send her
a good Dinner, a substantial Dinner, there's no fear of want of Stomachs
here, the air of this House is the thinnest and keenest in Europe. They that
can live upon our House-keeping, may surfeit upon the pickings of a Spaniards
Teeth. My Mistress, Sir, I doubt is a little of my Constitution, she loves
a good Meal.

speeches.speaker: Wrang.
prose:
Nothing but Cluttony and Intemperance goes down with you, Sirrah.
Had n't she two Sprats for Supper last night, and Oil to 'em too? Was n't
she sick with eating?

speeches.speaker: Fam.
prose:
Yes, she had Oil, and was sick with eating it, 'twou'd ha' turn'd a
Dutchman's Stomach; some Lamp or other furnish'd it.

speeches.speaker: Wrang.
prose:
Well, I'll have that Window stopt up; for I observe there are always
swarms of Bea^'s plying under it; as thick as Pimps, or Persons at
VVhitehall, or Porters at Billingsgate. Go call your Mistress, Sirrah.

speeches.speaker: VVrang.
prose:
Come, my Dear, I sent for thee from the Window in pure Tenderness,
the ^ too ^harp for thy delicate Constitution; thou shou'dst not
come ^ that Window, 'tis too bleak, and exposes thee too much to the
cold Wind; I'll stop it up.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
prose:
Come, I know your disease; 'tis your Jealousie, not your Affection
^ you ^ of me. How have I deserv'd to be mew'd thus like
^?

speeches.speaker: VVrang.
prose:
Retirement, my Florella, is the Pleasure of Life; Oh that I cou'd
enjoy what thou dost! that my affairs wou'd suffer me to be always with thee!
Privacy and good Housewifery are the best Ornaments of a Wife, a Vertuous
Woman, like a Rose, the less she's blown upon is the sweeter. Why shou'd
the Windows be open'd to let in Scandal, and Censure, when the wholsomest
Air blows inward.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
prose:
Of what use are the the sweetest Flowers, if none come near enough to
be refresh'd by, or perceive their Odours, yet they too only flourish in open air,
shut up they wither and die: So my Fame which might shine to the Honour
of us both, like a choak'd Lamp, is suffocated by your base Suspicions. No,
my Reputation which no malice cou'd ever touch, is tarnish'd by your Jealousie.
What occasion must the World imagine I've given for so severe a Confinement?

speeches.speaker: Fam.
prose:
Well said Mistress, to him agen; He has but little skill in
Husbandry I find; for I fancy his own House the fittest Soil in England to sow
Horns in; and I'm mistaken in my man, if he has n't brought home, as able a
Seeds-man.

speeches.speaker: VVrang.
prose:
Don't misconstrue my Love; thou'rt fair, my Dear, and the fairest
Flowers are soonest blasted. 'Tis not that I doubt thy Vertue; but the World is
envious, and I wou'd fence thee as well from its malice, as Temptations.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
prose:
If you believe me just and true, why daren't you trust me to my Liberty?
The seeds of Vertue thrive poorly in the shade, set 'em in the warm Sun, and
they spring gloriously. Why have n't I my Coach, rich Clothes, Jewels, and
Equipage, like other Lawyers Wives? Neither my Fortune, nor my Person are
inferiour to any of 'em; your sordid temper makes me vain, and tell you so.

speeches.speaker: VVrang.
prose:
Fye, Florella, don't take example by those foolish extravagant Women,
that stick their Husbands wealth upon 'em in trifles, and only mark out a
Gaudy Path to their own infamy and ruin.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
prose:
No such matter, they visit, and enjoy themselves, live plentifully and
merrily; and the indulgence of their kind Husbands binds them faster to 'em.

speeches.speaker: Fam.
prose: Well argu'd Mistress, keep your hold, Madam.

speeches.speaker: VVrang.
prose:
What is't you can desire, or wish? here's what may satisfie the
most covetous eye. Here are Diamonds, Rubies,
as fair as e're came from Ormus, or Bengal, worth Princes Ransomes, and Pearl,
as rich and orient, as Cleopatra's Banquet, all Nature's wealth, the Treasures
both of Sea and Land. Here's the work too of the most celebrated Artists,
Watches, Seals, Lockets, Rings, Crochets, and Neck-laces, that young Extravagants
purchase of Christian, and T^mpion, at the Price of their undoing;
where're they circulate, 'tis here they center, the reward and fruit of
honest industry, and good husbandry. All these are thine; what can they
show to vie with 'em, that carry all about 'em?

speeches.speaker: Flo.
prose:
And what am I the happier for all these? what use are they of to me,
more than if they were in the Mine? All this is but wealthy Beggary, and I
enjoy no more than starv'd Prisoners, Confinement, want and hunger. But
my Patience shall no longer bawd to my own misery. Here's a Treat, two Eggs,
and a Sallad, that wou'd n't give a single Caterpillar a Dinner.

speeches.speaker: Fam.
prose:
Nay, his Table's so loaded always, that his Cat's starv'd, and the Mice
have taken Sanctuary in the Church to avoid the same fate, and mend their
Quarters.

speeches.speaker: VVrang.
prose:
Come, prithee Dear, be satisfied, 'tis only my care of thy health; I
shou'd be loth, by our own thri^tless folly to become a constant Revenue to Doctors
and Apothecaries. Come, come, tho' what we have's but little, 'tis wholsome
and 'cleanly. I've been my self both Caterer, and Cook, Sweet.

speeches.speaker: Fam.
prose: A Pox o'th' Cook, that can't lick his Fingers.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
prose:
Can you think a Woman of my Birth and Fortune, can bear such usage
patiently? Such Avarice and Inhumanity? Is^t not enough that you're incapable
of being a Husband, but you must perform the Office of a Jaylor to confine
and starve me?

speeches.speaker: VVrang.
prose:
Come be pacified, and I'll add another Course to our Feast, you
shall have Milk, and stew'd Prunes for a Collation.

speeches.speaker: Fam.
prose: With Sugar to 'em, Sir.

speeches.speaker: VVrang.
prose:
This Rogue wou'd ruin our VVest India Plantations to fill but the
hollow of his sweet Tooth. Come, Florella, let's sit down, and think the Roman
Dainties at our Table; 'tis all but fancy.

speeches.speaker: Fam.
prose:
If that wou'd do, I've as strong a fancy to a good Meal, as the best of
them. Let the Devil take those ^gg-shells to equip his Witches for Lapland.
Now, in my opinion, 'tis Treason against all good Stomachs to hear a tedious
Grace said to no Meat. Well, I've a Rhadish yet, but that's transitory. I'll
steal off, and feast with it, upon the smell of the next Cook's Shop.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
prose: What Man was that you brought in with you?

speeches.speaker: Wrang.
prose:
A young Man, that is to study the Law under me, I've taken him
into the House, my Dear; but he sha'n't disturb thee, he sha'n't come near
thee, but at Meals. Did'st see him?

speeches.speaker: Flo.
prose: Yes, as you cross'd the yard together.

speeches.speaker: VVrang.
prose:
How dost like him? 'tis a silly, Bookish, Bashful wretch; but he
pays nobly, he desires but three Months Instructions, and he has given me
200 Guinea's before hand.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
prose:
I caren't for that, he sha'n't stay here. What a Life shall I lead betwixt
your Jealousie and Covetousness? whenever I see him, I shall be in fear of
one, or shame for 'tother.

speeches.speaker: VVrang.
prose:
O' my Conscience, thou need'st not apprehend either. He's such a
raw Phlegmatick cold thing, thou might'st wear him in thy Bosom, and n'er
warm him; his mind's o'th Law, and not on lewdness.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
prose:
Do, trust him, and repent it, do. I say he sha'n't stay, I know your
Jealous temper too well, I'll ha' no more of those fits.

speeches.speaker: VVrang.
prose:
Thou shalt n't, Dearest, I amn't Jealous of thee for any Man, much
less for him. Do but comply, and thou shalt have the profit of his Board to
buy thee Pins, which will be considerable; For he's willing to give any rate,
and yet so modest, that he's contented with the old Wood-room for a Lodging.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
prose:
That us'd to hold Fuel, now you've brought Fire into't, but 'tis your
own doing, and against my Opinion; Take notice therefore, if your Jealousie,
which is arrant Tinder, shou'd catch the Flame, I shall regard it only, as
an Ignis fatuus.

speeches.speaker: VVrang.
prose:
Fear nothing, Chicken, there's no danger; I'll call him to thee,
and thou sha't agree with him about the Terms thy self.

speeches.speaker: VVrang.
prose:
What, hard at it still? this is too violent to last, all things must
have their ^; Nature requires it. Come take breath, Sir, and consult your
health, as well as study. See how modest he is, speak to him, Wife, and encourage
him.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
prose:
Sir, you're welcome to such poor accommodation as our House can
afford.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose:
Thank ye, Madam, I'm not nice, any thing serves my turn; Books,
and your good Husband's Instructions are all my ambition.

speeches.speaker: VVran.
prose:
He's a very Book-worm, and feasts upon old Volumes, I must commit
him to your care, Wife; H's so bashful, he'l starve there else, before he'l
speak.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
prose:
Since 'tis your Pleasure, Sir, it shall be mine. And his too, or I mistake
my Man.

speeches.speaker: Fam.
prose:
'Sir, here are three Gentlemen desire to speake with you about earnest
business.

speeches.speaker: Wran.
prose:
I'll wait on 'em immediately.
Wife, make
much of my Pupil, and divert him, he's melancholy. He's the best
Client I've had these two Terms, not excepting my Lord Feewell. Encourage
him, and manage him smoothly, thou may'st get what thou wilt out of him.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
prose:
I shall get something for you then, you often dream of, but little think
so near you now. How long have you been destin'd for the Law,
Sir? You've too much Gravity for your years, you look wise, and dull
enough for a Recorder.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose:
I've lost abundance of precious time, Madam, and wou'd study hard to
redeem it, e'ry minute was invaluable, but they're past, and I wou'd employ
my utmost care to improve the remaining; 'tis that makes me so thoughtful,
not my natural temper.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
prose:
Come, you over-act your Part, I know you Friendly, this Disguise fits
as awkardly upon you, as the Hab. of a Non-Con Parson wou'd upon a Dancing
Master. Your Money has blinded him, he's easily impos'd upon, when he
gets by't. Tho' there's nothing more common, than for your Hypocrites in general
to cheat one another. But cou'd you imagin, that two years absence,
and this Disguise cou'd ^ide you from my Knowledge.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose:
My dear Florella,
thou art the only Volume
in the Lawyer's study, that I covet; let Wrangle tumble o're the rest,
and fill his head with Learned Jargon, Law Billingsgate, and scold from Cook
and Littleton to justifie his Knavery; let him ^ the Milch Purses of Litigious
Fools, I envy him nothing he enjoys, but thee.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
prose:
Hold Friendly, 'tis too much; I'm now another's right, and must not
grant, what I before might give, when 'twas my own; you freely had my
heart, my Body was another's purchase, who must alone enjoy it.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose:
Curse on your sordid Uncle, that ^ that, and yet with-held the rest.
He knew too well the Price, that Beauty yields, and wou'd n't truck for Love
or Hearts; but priz'd the Lot ^ I my then low Stock, then stept this
Muckworm in, out bid my ^ I'd the Ma^
.
^ and took Possession;
Curse on 'em both. But, ^ has been ki^der since, and given

me my Elder Brother's Estate; suffer me therefore to resume my right; and
since 'twas an unjust Purchase made o're my head, and in my wrong; thus,
thus I seize my own.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
prose:
O Friendly, but too well I love you, therefore as you tender my safety,
rake not into the ^mbers of our disquiet, nor seek to revive a Flame, that
will consume us both. I'm bound by Sacred Vows, and what Love prompts
me to, Duty forbids.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose:
Let not your Superstition wrong my Love, mistaken Notions, and
false Principles, not zeal for real duty, raise these doubts. The Matrimonial
Vow's reciprocal, as our Allegiance claims Protection, Conditions unperform'd
on either Part, make void the Obligation on 'tother. If you contract
with an insolvent Man for an Estate, are you bound to make good your Counter-part,
if he regards not his. Marriage is an agreement witness'd only, and
ratified by Law on certain terms, of which if he has fail'd, your Bond is cancell'd,
the Knot's dissolv'd, and you are mine again, by all the Canons both
of Church and Nature.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
prose:
Urge me no further, Friendly, 'tis a crime in me to hear you plead in
such a cause; But you've a Powerful Advocate within, that fain wou'd raise
rebellion in my Blood; down, down, thou Trayterous warmth, that swell'st
my Veins. How has my Husband fail'd, how forfeited?

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose:
As well may Winter boast the Summers Fruits, and chill December vie
with scorching July; as he pay down the Hymeneal dues, numb'd with the
Frost both of his Age and Temper, no Joy can spring through such an Icebound
Clay. This Air's too bleak for Love to wanton in; he seeks the cheerful
Sun to prune, and bask in, and keeps his Revels on warm Downy Beds, whose
Genial warmth revive, his drooping Joys. These, these, my dear Florella, shall be
thine, return but Love for Love at thy Devotion.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
prose:
Tempt me no more, too well you know your Power, and wou'd despise,
and hate me for my Frailty, shou'd you prevail. Why will you urge it
then?

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose: Dearest, charming Florella.

speeches.speaker: Fam.
prose: Madam, my Master's just at my Heels.

speeches.speaker: Wran.
prose:
How now Wife? What's the matter, Pupil? Why this disorder in
both your countenances? What's the meaning of this confusion? You look
angry, Sir; Why Sirrah, Famine, Rascal, what makes you run away?

speeches.speaker: Flo.
prose:
O! My Dear, I've committed such a Folly, such a Fault, I ne'r was
guilty of the like before. But 'tis your Fault, you—

speeches.speaker: Wran.
prose:
Why, what's the matter? what have ye done? tell me, speak quickly;
Have ye—

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose:
I'm ruin'd, discover'd, all my hope's lost, I shall be insulted
o're by Careless, and whooted at by all the Boys in Town.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
prose:
Such rudeness, such an Affront I've given this Gentleman, as I doubt
he n'er will pardon, and I can make no Apology for.

speeches.speaker: Wran.
prose:
I'm glad 'tis no worse, I had rather they shou'd quarrel than agree
too well, What have you done, how have you affronted him.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
prose:
He mentioning New England, and I not dreaming he was of that Country,
I told him some Stories of that Place, which I have formerly heard my

Cousin Ramble tell; His Colour went, and came, he look'd first Pale, then
Red, then Pale, and Red again, which I not thinking him concern'd, ne^r
minded imputing it only to his excessive Bashfulness till by the extream disorder,
and confusion I perceiv'd him under, I found it touch'd him nearer.

speeches.speaker: Wran.
prose:
'Twas indiscreetly done, but like a Woman, rather than want Tattle,
to out with all they know at first sight to any Body. Sir, you must pardon
her; you must follow the rule of Law, in like cases, where if any Persons
offend without malice, or ill design, they are acquitted; you'l find it in
your reading; 'tis call'd Chance-medley. See an' he ben't discompos'd still.
Why Wife, ask his Pardon, Wife.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose:
Sir, your Lady's not in fault, 'tis my misfortune, that there's too much
truth in what was said, which I had not temper enough to cover my concern
for. But I beg to be excus'd the uneasie repetition of Particulars.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
prose:
Sir, I ask your Pardon, and will hereafter offend you in that manner
no more.

speeches.speaker: Wran.
prose:
Come, come, all's well, we'l drink a Glass to a better understanding,
and bid my Pupil welcome; come you'l agree the better hereafter, as
Bones once broken knit the closer.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose: I hope thou'rt a Prophet, Lawyer?

speeches.speaker: Wran.
prose: Fam^ne.
Did you call, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Wran.
prose: Fetch the Bottle, and the ^l^ss out of my Writing-Desk.

speeches.speaker: Fam.
prose: The Ink-Bottle, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Wran.
prose: No, the Bottle of He^rts-ease, Sirrah, and wash the Glass.

speeches.speaker: Fam.
prose: Shall I tye a String to't, Sir? it may be swallow'd unawares else.

speeches.speaker: Wran.
prose: Away, Sirrah, and do as I bid you, here's the Key.

speeches.speaker: Wran.
prose:
Come, fill a Glass, it warms the Stomach, and moderately us'd is
Cordial, too much destroys Health, and ruins the strongest Constitution.
Come Pupil to ye;—How thou fill'st Villain!—This Rogue's in League
with some Apothecary sure to throw us all into Fevers.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose:
A very little, pray; I'm not us'd to strong Liquors. Madam,
to your best Thoughts.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
prose:
They're at present how to make you reparation, Sir. Come, Dearest,
Success to the Gentleman's undertaking, that his Studies may thrive.

speeches.speaker: Wran.
prose: 'Tis a good wish, he sha'n't want my Assistance.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose: I thank you both for these undeserv'd favours.

speeches.speaker: Wran.
prose:
I've been reconciling two Quarrelsome Neighbours, they had no
Money, so I e'en advis'd 'em to a Reference; 'tis the best way of ending
poor Causes. 'Tis for rich Booties, Golden Birds, we spread the Nets o'th
Law. Ha'ye agree'd on the rate.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
prose:
He offers more than I can in Conscience take, or you
desire.

speeches.speaker: Wran.
prose:
Phoo, Phoo, Scruples are Bug-bears for Children:
Be wise, and close with him.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
prose: Well, since you advise it, I will.

speeches.speaker: Wran.
prose:
Come, my Dear, thou canst sing, give my Pupil one Song, and
then leave us to discourse of his Studies.

verse:
A SONG by a Lady.
WHy was not Wit with Beauty joyn'd?
I hate ^ Face without a Mind.
If e're I to that Sex submit,
'Twill be to Cloe's powerful Wit.
For Coelia, tho' divinely fair,
Art may improve, or Age impair.
When Wit alone, my Passion moves!
The only thing which Time improves.
The God with Wit must tip his dart,
And pierce my Ear, to wound my Heart.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose:
Sir, I am very sensible, that the Business of a Lawyer depends not
wholly ^on Learning, or great reading in the Law, there are other mea
^
^ be ^ to introduce a Man to Practice.

You observe very well; For in our Profession, as in all others, 'tis
^ m^it, but a little unheeded, artificial management, that recommends us
^ the world, and gets Business, tho the thoughtless croud impute it to our
^ill and Ability. So the City-Divines insinuate themselves into the favour of
the People, by Preaching up Popular Doctrines, and declaiming for Liberty
and Property, the Contract implied betwixt the King and Subject in the
Oaths of Coronation and Allegiance, and the lawfulness of Rebellion upon
disgust, and the necessity of curbing the Prerogative; at Court they raise
themselves by advancing the Divine Right of Monarchy, and urging the
dangerous consequences of disobedience, and making Resistance to the Higher
Powers, and enforcing the Religious Obligation to the Civil Authority,
and the danger of using our own Eyes, and consulting Carnal Reason in
matter of Faith. The circumstances of Time and Place are nicely to be consider'd;
For that which is Orthodox at Whitehall, is seldom calculated for the
Meridian of Cheapside.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose:
Nay, the Spiritual Compass in that respect is like the Mariners and the
Priests, like their Needles, tho' they agree in their main aim, have their several
Points at which they certainly vary.

speeches.speaker: Wrang.
prose:
In Physick, the Doctors grow famous by affronting Galen and
Hippocrates, and complementing Apothecaries; by writing long Bills fill'd
with unnecessary Medicines; by repeating Draughts, Bolus's, and Pearl Cordials,
and emptying the Patients Pockets to fill their Windows; by caresling
Old Midwives, and bribing Nurses, and Favourite Servants; by making
impertinent officious Visits. Philosophical Gossipings, and talking Non-sense
liberally to Old Ladies in Cramp Terms; by commending the insipid Receipts
they show 'em, and communicating now and then a Dispensatory Water
for an Arcanura of their own; by reading in their Coaches what they
don't understand in their Studies; by running into Cabals to recommend
their own Faction, and decrying the rest of their Profession; by frequenting Conventicles,
and Lecture-Sermons to please Knaves, and cheat Fools into an Opinion

of their Religion; by talking perpetually of Monstrosities, and unusual
Phoenomena, tho' at the same time they can't distinguish betwixt a Chamoelion,
and a Dutch Sooterkin. These are the Acts that make 'em famous, 'tis no matter
for Learning, they need not cure, if they can but amuse the People; A
Collection of Journals, or Transactions equips 'em for Philosophers, a Slaughter-house
for Anatomists, and their Grand-mothers for Chymists.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose:
Well, there are Cheats in all Trades, not excepting ours; and I find
'tis easier much to be a Man of Business, than a Man of Skill. I've lost so much
time in New England, that I wou'd fain take the shortest cut to the Knowledge
and Practice of the Law. For that end I desir'd to be plac'd under your
Instructions; whatever you are pleas'd to communicate, shall be further acknowledg'd.

speeches.speaker: Wrang.
prose:
You say honestly; and I'll deal by you like a Son, I'll let you into
all the Mysteries of our Art, and if you can but follow my Directions,
I'll make you a Master of it too, one Month in my House shall be worth
seven years in your Study.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose:
Sir, you bind me to you, and doubt not but by your good Lectures
to prove such a Proficient, as you need not be asham'd on.

speeches.speaker: Wrang.
prose:
Most Gentlemen take a wrong method in breeding their Sons to
the Law, they send 'em to the Inns of Court, where, if they prove Students,
(which very few do) they drudge away seven years, in making common
Place-Books from Reports, and Statute-Books, before they're call'd to the
Bar; and many saunter away seven, and seven more, before they be sent to't
again with a Fee.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose:
My Father was very sensible of that, which made him take other
measures.

speeches.speaker: Wrang.
prose:
He's a wise Man, I warrant him; For with an experienc'd Practiser,
you shall learn more thriving Law in a few Months, than in your whole
Life in a Study, if he will be free and communicate, which any one will do
upon a good consideration.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose:
That sha'nt be wanting, Sir, my Father has taken care for that, and I'll
see his Commands perform'd.

speeches.speaker: Wrang.
prose:
You do wisely both. But to be successful in our Profession, there
is an aptness of Temper requir'd. Some Men set up for such a scrupulous, inflexible
honesty, that they are n't to be mov'd an Inch from what they call
their duty upon any consideration, that start, and boggle at the hast oblique
Proposition. Have nothing to do with 'em, not one in a hundred of 'em,
proves worth a farthing. Do you love Money heartily?

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose:
Entirely, I never part with it, but to get more of it, or something more
valuable, as I hope to do now.

speeches.speaker: Wrang.
prose:
Very good. Then you need not pore upon Law-Books continually,
and cite Cases as some do; a moderate skill in Law-terms, and a com^
knowledg of the common Practice of the several Coats will carry you
through all, with a little Address, which I'll teach you.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose: Under so great a Master 'tis impossible to miscarry.

speeches.speaker: Wrang.
prose:
When you're call'd to the Bar, you must make an interest in some
Attornies and Solicitors, which you may easily do by letting 'em ^ in
all the Fees, they bring you, and giving 'em Authority to use your ^

when e're they've occasion for a Councel's Hand without a Fee, which they
frequently have. These things may seem at first to lessen your profit; but
trust me they return with Interest upon Interest.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose:
But how must I behave my self at the Bar, when I come there; for if
Law ben't necessary, I suppose, there must be other Qualifications in its stead.

speeches.speaker: Wrang.
prose:
You're young, and seem to have good strong Lungs; are you well
breath'd? are you long winded?

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose:
Very long winded, when I was a Boy, I cou'd out-holloa e're a Hunter
in New England.

speeches.speaker: Wrang.
prose:
Tis the best Qualification for the Bar in the World. Then when
you're retain'd in any Cause, be sure you talk enough, talk abundance, no
matter what; if you. can outwind the Antagonist's Councel, your Points gain'd.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose: But will the Court suffer that? won't the Bench take notice of it.

speeches.speaker: Wrang.
prose:
No matter for that, you must n't be easily snub'd, if the Court give
you a Check, go on still; and if at last they force you to desist, sit down
sullenly, and say not a word more in the cause, if it ^oes for you, your
Client will hug you, and attribute all his success to your zeal at first; if
otherwise he'l impute it to the partiality of the Judge that wou'd n't hear you
out. There's Councellor Noisie is one of the best Lawyers for that, that ever
tir'd the Court.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose: I've heard much of your Fame, Sir, for this Politick way of Practice.

speeches.speaker: Wrang.
prose:
Time has been Pupil; but my Lungs are past the best, they won't
serve me now as they have done. You'l be of a rare Age for it, when you
come to't. When your Adversarie's Witnesses are call'd, be sure to give 'em
frequent Interruptions by Questions, sly cunning Questions, there's a great
deal of Art in managing an Adversarie's Witness well; by neat address most
of 'em may be made Evidences for you; but you must ask 'em cunningly;
you may lead 'em whither you please, and draw what answers you will from
'em. But if the adverse Councel discover and countermine you, to cross Purposes
with 'em immediately, ask 'em Questions innumerable to the Point or
not, 'tis all one, it confounds 'em, confounds the Court, and perplexes the
Cause.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose:
But how must we do to defend our own Witnesses from the same Practice
o't'other side?

speeches.speaker: Wrang.
prose:
They must be prepar'd before hand; a well-instructed Witness is all
in all. 'Twou'd make a Man mad to see what Witnesses are brought out of the
Country sometimes, there's no hammering a right impression in their heads.
If you wou'd have a Cause go glibly forward, never trouble those thick skull'd
Rogues, but take two or three of your own training, or that you've try'd;
and I'll warrant your Cause for miscarrying.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose: But are they so easie to be had?

speeches.speaker: Wrang.
prose:
There are about this Town abundance of very pretty apt fellows,
that either through a natural inclination to appear in publick, or their necessities,
are very ready to receive any Impression from Money.

speeches.speaker: Fam.
prose:
Sir, there's Madam Olympia, and Mr. Affidavit without, and desire to
speak with you.

speeches.speaker: Wrang.
prose:
Wait on. 'em in. Nay, you

may stay Pupil, we may have occasion for your Hand. This Mr. Affidavit's
the ablest Solicitor in England, he has always his Witnesses, and his Implements
in such order, 'twou'd do one's heart good to be of Councel for him.

speeches.speaker: Wrang.
prose:
Madam, I'm your Ladiships most humble Servant, the 10000l. was
paid to me yesterday according to your Order; How will your Ladiship be
pleas'd to have it dispos'd of?

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose:
That's what I'm come about Mr. Serjeant; I've two or three offers, and
am in some doubt which to take, they all appear fair.

speeches.speaker: Affid.
prose:
Does your Ladiship persist in your resolution of accepting an Assignment
of Squire Careless's Mortgage, there can be no better Security in the
World.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose:
I wish she wou'd, she's a Woman of Honour, and Careless may expect
kindness and civil Treatment from her; but I'm afraid these Knaves will trick
her; I'll watch 'em.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose:
If Mr. Serjeant will use me well, I'm willing enough; for I don't care
to break the Sum, and 'tis too big to lend upon any, but Land-Security.

speeches.speaker: Wrang.
prose:
Madam, I'll ask nothing of you for my Bargain; Pay me my Principal
and Interest at seven per Cent. which is the Interest Mr. Careless shou'd
have paid, and 'tis your Ladiships.

speeches.speaker: Aff.
prose:
Take him at's word, Madam; if I had the Money to lay down, as
you have, I'd not take 5000l. for my Bargain, as I cou'd manage it. Your
Ladiship may afford the Serjeant's Lady a Present of a Noble Piece of Plate.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose:
You might perhaps, but I can't. Whenever Mr. Careless, or his Friends,
think fit to redeem it, I shall take no advantage.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose: 'Tis nobly answer'd, and Careless shall know his Obligation to thee.

speeches.speaker: Aff.
prose:
How foolishly some People throw away these Golden Opportunities,
but that I know the Serjeant too well, I cou'd make a shift to raise the Money.
But we Sharpers never play with one another.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: What's the Sum, Mr. Serjeant?

speeches.speaker: Wrang.
prose:
The Principal, Madam, 17000l. the Interest 3500l. and some odd
Pounds, but you shall know to a Farthing.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose:
Well, let the Writings be drawn that they may be perus'd by my
Councel, and the rest of your Money shall be ready upon Sealing.. Mr. Serjeant
where's your Lady, I must see her; why won't she visit me sometimes?
I almost take it ill.

speeches.speaker: Wrang.
prose:
She stirs so little abroad, she's not fit to wait upon your Ladiship.
Famine, bid your Mistress wait upon her Ladiship immediately.

speeches.speaker: Wrang.
prose: Ha! what Noise is that?

speeches.speaker: Aff.
prose: 'Tis the Clashing of Swords sure, keep the Door fast.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose: What's the matter, Sir? y'are not hurt I hope.

speeches.speaker: Car.
prose:
No, thanks to your timely Inter^ Sir; my worst hurt is, my
Regret, for having been the ^ fair Lady.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
prose:
If my Fright has ^ in the safety of a Gentleman.
'tis very welcome to me.

speeches.speaker: Car.
prose:
I'm a stranger, Madam, to that sweet voice, yet I'm glad to hear it
sound a more pleasing Note.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: May a Woman be so bold as to ask the occasion of this Quarrel, Sir?

speeches.speaker: Car.
prose:
The Serjeant there, Madam, or Mr. Affidavit, can better resolve that
Question than I; these were some of their Mirmydons, I suppose, they
were Catchpoles, Bayliffs, Madam.

speeches.speaker: Wrang.
prose: Upon my word. Mr. Careless, 'twas n't at my Suit.

speeches.speaker: Aff.
prose: Nor any, that I know of, I do assure you, Sir.

speeches.speaker: Car.
prose: Well then you two ha' got enough by me; will you be my Bail?

speeches.speaker: Wrang.
prose:
Indeed, Sir, you must excuse me, you know you're a great many
thousand Pounds in my debt, and pay no Interest, you take no care o'that.

speeches.speaker: Car.
prose:
Don't you take care o'that? Don't you receive my Rents. Thou perplexer
of Causes, thou tormenter of the Law, the Stomach of an Ostriege is
but a Type of thy Conscience, that can digest any thing, tho' never so hard
and bulky. Canst thou swallow three thousand Pounds a year, and disgorge
nothing? I don't owe you any thing, Sir; do I?

speeches.speaker: Aff.
prose:
No, Sir, but I've made a solemn resolution never to Bail any Man,
tho' he were my Father. Besides, we don't know at whose Suit, nor for what
this Action is brought.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose: I've enquir'd that, 'tis at the Suit of one Mr. Snip, a Taylor, for 70l.

speeches.speaker: Aff.
prose: Sir, I'm sorry I can't serve you in this Affair, in any thing else—

speeches.speaker: Car.
prose:
Why thou Buckram Bag-Carrier, thou Bastard, Son of Parchment,
thou Nit to the Lay, thou Cur that art grown fat upon the scatterings of my
Extravagance, dar'st thou bark at me? your Man his scarce worn out the Livery
that came off your own Back; and dare you insult? Of all my Follies,
or misfortunes this is the worst, that I shou'd want, or expect any kindness
from such Grubs, such groveling Muck worms.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: A brave spirited, mettl'd Fellow.

speeches.speaker: Car.
prose:
But I'll take care to provide such ^ine for you, Horse le^ches, as
shall make you discharge the Go^ you swell with, I will ye Blood suckers,
I will.

speeches.speaker: Fr.
prose:
Here take this Ring and ^awn it to him, 'tis worth two hundred
Pound, to morrow you shall redeem it.

speeches.speaker: Flo.
prose:
Pray, my Dear, oblige the Gentleman, 'tis in your own power to repay
your self.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose:
Mr. Serjeant, you ought not to let the Gentl^man suffer, since you
with-hold his Estate.

speeches.speaker: Wrang.
prose:
So, h'as brought the Women over to his Party already, a handsome,
wild young Fellow, ^'r misses their good word.

speeches.speaker: Car.
prose:
Ladies, I'm extremly oblig'd to you both for this Favour; your
Beauties ought to command, not su^: But to such a fordid Wretch I've a better
Advocate, one that ^, and ^hin^s with ^ Lustre in his greedy ^yes,
than all the Charms you are Mistresses of. Here, Lawyer;
I know you love ^ Security: You understand these Things. ^'er look
a-skew, Man; 'tis right, and cost Two Hundred ^. What dare you
^nd upon't?

speeches.speaker: Wran.
prose:
I don't care to meddle with such things; I don't know the Value
of 'em.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose:
Lend him 200l. upon't, and place it to my Account, and give
me the Ring, and Bail him, and I'll indemnifie you.

speeches.speaker: Wran.
prose:
Well, Madam; if you'll secure me, it shall be done.. Now, Sir; after all these Provocations and Indignities, you may
justly expect I shou'd insult o'er your Necessities: But, to let you see how little
those Indecencies your Passion has made you utter, have affected me, I'll
lend you 200l. upon your Ring, which shall be yours again whenever you
please to redeem it; and will be your Bail to this Action. Mr. Affidavit, pray
call in the Officer; but let his Followers keep without.

speeches.speaker: Car.
prose:
For the Money, you've a Pledge, I sha'n't part with; and for the rest,
you know how to lick your self whole.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose:
Still brave, and like himself: He can't return Thanks for a Service, he
does n't think done out of Kindness.

speeches.speaker: Fler.
prose:
I shall be a Widow suddenly, I hope: This Generosity looks like a
Lightning before Death.

speeches.speaker: Friend.
prose: Heaven verifie the Omen, Madam.

speeches.speaker: Wran.
prose:
O, Mr. Trappum! Are you the Man? Pray, What Summ's this
Action for? What's the Debt? and at whose Suit?

speeches.speaker: Off.
prose: The Debt's 70l. and at Mr. Snip's Suit.

speeches.speaker: Wran.
prose:
Well, I'll be th^ Gentleman's Bail: You'll take my Word till anon,
and not molest him?

speeches.speaker: Off.
prose: An't were for 1000l. an't please your Worship.

speeches.speaker: Wran.
prose:
Well, call two or three Hours hence, and the Business shall be
done.

speeches.speaker: Off.
prose: God bless your Worship; 'Servant, Master.

speeches.speaker: Wran.
prose: Sir, I'll fetch your Money.

speeches.speaker: Car.
prose:
Ladies, this wonderful Conversion's owing to your Charms; your
Eyes are the happiest S^ars e'er influenc^d my Fortune.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
Flor.
prose:
Mine, Madam, have shed their Influence long since: 'Tis for your
Ladyship, to work such strange Conversions.

speeches.speaker: Car.
prose:
I shall impute it to the happy Conjunction of Both. Had I only such
bright Constellations to consult, I should turn Astrologer, and ne'er be out in
my Predictions.

speeches.speaker: Wran.
prose:
I must break off this Parley, that extravagant Fellow will sollicite my
Wife before my Face else. Sir, here's your Money; 'tis all Gold,
except a little Silver to make the Samm even.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose:
Mr. Serjeant, You'll take care to dispatch those Writings as fast as you
can? But don't let Mr. Careless know a Syllable.

speeches.speaker: Wran.
prose: I'll wait upon your Ladyship with'em, in a few Hours.

speeches.speaker: Ol.
prose: Mr. Serjeant, your Servant: Madam, your most humble Servant.

speeches.speaker: Car.
prose:
Your Ladyship will permit me to wait upon you to your Coach? Madam,
your humble Servant: Gentlemen, yours.

speeches.speaker: Wran.
prose:
Come, let's walk in: Mr. Affidavit, I ha' further Business with
you.

speeches.speaker: Friend.
verse: I dare not yet to such Conversions trust,
Where M^sers gen'rous prove, and Knaves are just.
prose:
For my part, I can't believe this Miracle; there's some deeper
laid Knavery, than I can fathom the Bottom of: I'll follow'em, and try
what Discovery may be made.

speeches.speaker: Car.
prose:
CAN you guess the meaning, Friendly, of the Lawyer's surprizing
Change? If ill Language and Railing work so well with him, I'll
make my self Master of all the Rhetorick of Billingsgate, to pleasure him; the
best Breath'd, loudest Scold there, shall be a civil, modest Person to me.

speeches.speaker: Friend.
prose:
That's a Groundless Fancy. Quarrelling's his Trade, and Scolding
his daily Exercise at the Bar; 'tis as familiar to him as Snuff to an Irish-man,
and he takes it as unconcernedly. If you had as much Malice as a disappointed
She-Saint, as much Scandal as a Secret Historian, with the Lungs and Front of
a Scotch Field-Preacher, you'd ne'er be able to rail him out of a single Doit.
There's some Roguery a foot, which I'd fain trace.

speeches.speaker: Car.
prose:
Why shou'd he send the Ring back without Money? He knows I'm
too sensble of his Knavery, for him to trust to my Honour. There's the
Ring, Friendly, and my Thanks.

speeches.speaker: Friend.
prose:
This is none of my Ring; 'tis a fairer, and worth more than mine.
Here, take't again, and wear it: We're in a Labyrinth now, and this may
prove a Clue to guide us out again.

speeches.speaker: Car.
prose:
What! more Miracles? Nay, e'en keep it till I redeem yours. Sure
some Qualm of Conscience has o'ertaken this harpy Serjeant; some honest
Devil or other has frighted him into a Fit of Repentance, and he begins to
refund now with the same Grace that Thieves make Restitution at the Gallows.
Oh, for your Spiritual Pimp now, to perfect this good Work of the
Devil's beginning.

speeches.speaker: Friend.
prose:
^'m apt to think the Flesh has more to do in this Matter, than the
Devil. I fancy I'm Oedipus enough to solve this Riddle. Who brought this
King?

speeches.speaker: Car.
prose:
I don't know: 'Twas sent to me, at the R^se, seal'd up, and superscrib'd,
but nothing written within the Paper: Before I cou'd come out of
the Room, the ^essenger was gone.

speeches.speaker: Friend,
prose:
Let's see the S^al; something may be made of that perhaps.
What's here? A Lady throwing out a Rope to a drowning Cupid! More
Mystery still! Do you understand Hieroglyphicks, Careless?

speeches.speaker: Car.
prose:
Not very well; but I can guess at this. Faith, Friendly, I'm sorry
to be thy Rival: I suppose the Serjeant's Lady has taken a Fancy to my Person,
and either rob'd or whead^'d her Husband out of this Ring, and sent it
me, as an Earnest of her Inclination. 'Tis as unwelcome as Press-Money to me;

I don't like the Service, for your sake: Prithee keep it, and serve for me.
Pox on't, this Clerk-like Figure thou mak'st, disgusts her.

speeches.speaker: Friend.
prose:
No, take it again: You're mistaken; 'tis one that can draw surer
and deeper than Florella. What think you of the Widow Olympia?

speeches.speaker: Car.
prose: I remember she pleaded for me to the Lawer, indeed.

speeches.speaker: Friend.
prose:
I can tell you more than that; she has taken your Estate into her
Care, and perhaps designs as much for your Person.

speeches.speaker: Car.
prose:
If she's any Design, my Body's at her Devotion; an easie Fine shall
make her Mistress of it: But I don't care for making a Settlement, or granting
too long a Lease.

speeches.speaker: Friend.
Car.
prose:
I'm afraid I'm more likely to be the Mouse; if this Female Pufs shou'd
get me into her Clutches, you must rescue me, Friendly; you must be my
Deliverer.

speeches.speaker: Friend.
prose:
Ne'er fear, Man; if she does, she'll use you like a Kitten. What
a faint-hearted Soldier art thou, to shrink before the Enemy comes in view!

speeches.speaker: Car.
prose:
A prudent General wou'd be cautious of bringing himself under a Necessity
of Engaging where the Success is doubtful, and ev'n Victory is certain Loss.

speeches.speaker: Friend.
prose:
What careful Officer wou'd not quit Quarters that lie waste; and
venture something to win a rich Soil, with a great Crop standing, and plentiful
Magazins?

speeches.speaker: Car.
prose:
But no wise Commander wou'd fight himself into a Nook, tho' never
so rich, to be penn'd in there, who'd all the rest of the Country to forage in
at liberty. These Women of Honour expect such a deal of Constancy and
Sincerity, that I dare not venture on'em. I can't swim, and therefore care
no more to Love, than wash out of my Depth; I should be lost if I did.

speeches.speaker: Friend.
prose:
These raw Lovers are like fearful Boys, that put first one Foot into
the Water, then t'other, and so prolong their Pain; when 'tis but plunging
boldly to be out on't.

speeches.speaker: Car.
prose:
Yes, yes; you that are in, cry 'tis warm, to draw more Fools after
you: But we that are dry and warm on Shoar, have no reason to trust to such
shivering, chattering Invitations.

speeches.speaker: Car.
prose:
Here comes your starv'd Pimp: 'Twou'd puzzle a nice Virtuoso to
tell which weighs most, he, or his Shadow. How now, Shotten Herring?

speeches.speaker: Friend.
prose: How is't, Famine? What Wind blew thee hither?

speeches.speaker: Fam.
prose:
Faith, a brisk Wind might blow me like a Feather, Sir: I've ballasted
my Stomach well out of your Bounty; otherwise, the least Blast would have
over-set me: I was afraid to venture into the Sun, for-fear of being drawn
up among the Motes that play in the Beams.

speeches.speaker: Friend.
prose:
Well, mind my Business, and thou shalt fare better than my Lord
Mayor's Carver; thy Belly shall be all thy Care, and thou shalt out-feed a Catholick
Priest at Easter.

speeches.speaker: Fam.
prose:
Shall I see good Days, Days of Plenty again? Then hang this penurious
Master of mine; let him eat his Cheese unpar'd, and eat the Rhind of
his Bacon himself; I'll no more of 'em. If you'll but provide for my Belly
well, you shall furnish his Head as you please.

speeches.speaker: Friend.
prose:
Thou shalt be fat and Iusty, Si^rah; it shall be Carnival all the Year:
Effect but this, thou shalt be-rich too.

speeches.speaker: Fam.
prose:
Hang Money, Sir, 'tis mercenary; Give me Meat plenty, and drink
